newsitem.title: UK: Rare Sinn Fein-Unionist TV debate ahead of talks.
newsitem.headline: Rare Sinn Fein-Unionist TV debate ahead of talks.

text.p: Television stages a rehearsal of what Northern Ireland's peace talks could be like when two of its most outspoken political opponents meet head to head for the first time in the British province on Tuesday.

The late-night debate brings into the ring Ken Maginnis, a leading member of the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), and Martin McGuinness, chief negotiator of the Irish Republican Army's political wing, Sinn Fein.
The two men have traded pro- and anti-British barbs over the airwaves for years but never in the same Northern Ireland studio. Now they will, in advance of historic peace talks in September.

The UUP's decision to take part in the discussion marks a change in direction by Northern Ireland's biggest political party, which has hitherto shunned all contact with what it calls an extension of IRA guerrillas.

Maginnis, security spokesman for the UUP, has in the past accused McGuinness and his party of being apologists for the IRA's 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland and of being inextricably involved in it.
Tuesday's debate takes place three weeks after the IRA called a new ceasefire to get Sinn Fein to peace talks to chart a way out of a conflict that has killed 3,200.

But the UUP is far from certain to sit down at the same negotiating table when the talks begin in earnest on September 15 because it wants the IRA to prove its war is over for good by handing over some of its guns and semtex plastic explosive.

McGuinness, a veteran Irish republican based in the Irish nationalist stronghold of Londonderry, is on record as saying that he has no reason to believe the IRA will hand over a single bullet until a final settlement is agreed.

The issue of "arms decommissioning" is expected to dominate the debate as it has in a year of preparation for the start of substantive talks on a new constitutional set-up for Northern Ireland in September.

Two unionist parties walked out of the talks altogether in protest at Anglo-Irish proposals that the IRA and its Protestant loyalist foes be allowed to surrender weapons as the talks progress, rather than before or at the end.

But David Trimble's UUP says it will stay at the talks although it has yet to clarify whether it will actually sit down at the same table with representatives of a party it accuses of being a front for Europe's most formidable guerrilla army.

The UUP has appeared on U.S. television shows twice before with UUP representatives but the countdown to what Britain and Ireland say is the best chance of negotiating peace in a generation has given the debate added ratings potential.

Maginnis, a former schoolteacher, policeman and part-time British army major, is the silver-haired spokesman the UUP uses to shoot down Sinn Fein pronouncements. He says the IRA truce is just a ruse to get to the peace talks.

He is expected to argue, using his own intelligence sources, that the IRA will review the truce in four months time and go back to war if it believes that the negotiations will not lead to the united Ireland it seeks.

McGuinness frequently denies allegations that he is or was a senior figure in the IRA's leadership and will argue that the UUP has nothing to fear and should embrace the concept of a united Ireland because it is inevitable.
Britain and Ireland say Northern Ireland's British status will not change until a majority wants it. The region's Protestant majority favours continued ties with Britain.
But Sinn Fein says the province is a colonial remnant and the talks should begin dismantling it in preparation of a merger with Ireland.
